definition: An N-jet is the set of (partial) derivatives of a function f ( x ) {\displaystyle f(x)} up to order N.
details: Specifically, in the area of computer vision, the N-jet is usually computed from a scale space representation L {\displaystyle L} of the input image f ( x , y ) {\displaystyle f(x,y)} , and the partial derivatives of L {\displaystyle L} are used as a basis for expressing various types of visual modules. For example, algorithms for tasks such as feature detection, feature classification, stereo matching, tracking and object recognition can be expressed in terms of N-jets computed at one or several scales in scale space.

explainer.lead: An N-jet bundles a function's partial derivatives up to order N, giving a compact local description of how an image or signal changes. In computer vision it provides a common basis for expressing feature detection, classification, matching and recognition.

tiers.eli5: Think of describing a hill not just by its height but also its slope, curvature and finer bends; an N-jet collects all those measurements up to a chosen level of detail.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers compute N-jets from a scale-space representation of the image and use the derivatives as building blocks for visual modules; a common pitfall is that higher-order derivatives amplify noise, so scale selection matters.
tiers.paperLevel: The N-jet of f(x) is the set of its partial derivatives up to order N; in vision it is usually computed from a scale-space representation L of the image f(x,y), and its computational cost and noise sensitivity grow with N.

explainer.example: For N=2 on a 2-D image, the jet holds the value, the two first derivatives and the three second derivatives at a point, from which a blob or edge detector can be built.
